title: Kune Food's Last Day, With 55,000 Meals Sold and No Next Round
dek: In June 2022 the founder of a Nairobi ready-meal start-up closed it in public, apologised to those who had trusted it, and asked other firms to hire his staff.

story.event: Closing a Nairobi ready-meal start-up after failing to raise its next round
story.summary: Kune Food, a Nairobi cloud kitchen founded by Robin Reecht in December 2020 and backed by a $1 million pre-seed round in 2021, closed on 22 June 2022 after failing to raise a planned $3.5 million round as food costs rose. About 90 people lost their jobs. Reecht announced the closure on LinkedIn, apologised to staff, investors, suppliers and customers, offered references for his team and invited offers for the company's assets.
paragraphs: On 22 June 2022 Robin Reecht called Kune Food's staff to an unscheduled meeting and told them the company was closing, The Star reported. Then he wrote on LinkedIn: "Sad day. Kune Food closed down today." About ninety people lost their jobs. TechCrunch reported that some had been hired only the month before.

Reecht had moved from France to Nairobi in November 2020. He told TechCrunch that three days after he arrived, people told him good food at a low price was impossible to find, and in December he founded Kune to sell ready meals cooked in its own kitchen. It began, he later wrote, with him and a chef carrying meals on foot to a nearby office. In June 2021 Kune raised a $1 million pre-seed round led by Launch Africa Ventures, took a bank loan and built a factory. Its launch drew criticism from Kenyans who pointed to the city's many affordable eateries, and Kune apologised for how his remarks had come across.

By mid-2022 Kune had a factory, a kitchen studio, a tech platform and seven distribution hubs, and had moved from its own riders to Uber Eats, Glovo and Bolt Food. Since January it had sold more than 55,000 meals to more than 6,000 individual customers and 100 companies. Earlier in the year it had said it was raising $3.5 million to expand. That round did not come, while Kenyan food prices reached record highs. "But at $3 per meal," Reecht wrote, "it just wasn't enough to sustain our growth."

He blamed the downturn, tightening investment markets and food costs, and did not spare himself. His post turned first to the team: he urged other founders to look through Kune's LinkedIn employee page and offered references. He apologised to suppliers, customers, bankers and partners, and told investors, "To betray your confidence is something for which I will never forgive myself." Many things, he wrote, could have been done differently. He invited offers for Kune's intellectual property and assets, and said he would reflect on the failure before saying more.

quote.text: That I may not suffer two evils: one, the loss of my money; another, the reproach of my neighbor
quote.locator: Chapter IV, "On the Benefit of Being Silent", Story II
quote.source_title: The Persian Literature, Volume 2 (The Gulistan, tr. James Ross), Project Gutenberg eBook #13060
quote.connection: Saadi's merchant, having lost a thousand dinars, tells his son to keep quiet so the loss is not doubled by gossip. Reecht chose the second loss: he closed in public, apologised to each group he had let down, and gave his staff's job search the same audience.

reflection: There is real sense in Saadi's merchant. A loss told to the wrong people grows, and Reecht's launch had already drawn public criticism. He spoke anyway, and the people who most needed him to speak were the ninety who now had to find work.

You will have your own smaller versions of this: a plan that did not work, a result you got wrong, a week that went badly. Not every loss needs announcing. But when other people are carrying part of it, saying so early and plainly is often the only help you can still give them.
invitation: If something you lead has gone wrong this month, decide who is carrying part of the cost. Tell one of them today what happened, in two sentences, without dressing it up.

research_notes: Date: the slate gave 2023; every source dates the closure to 22 June 2022, so the story uses that. Operating time: TechCrunch and The Star say about a year; Citizen Digital and Kenyans.co.ke headlines say ten months (from the August 2021 launch); TechMoran says commercial operations began about four months earlier; The Standard says six months after a February launch. The story avoids a length and gives the founding (December 2020) and funding (June 2021) dates. Pre-seed in shillings: Ksh107 million (Kenyans.co.ke body), Ksh100 million (its headline), Ksh112 million (Citizen Digital); the story uses $1 million. TechMoran says Kune 'raised' $3.5 million, against TechCrunch and Citizen Digital, which say it was raising that sum, and Reecht's own statement that it could not raise its next round; the story follows Reecht and TechCrunch. Bizna Kenya (not cited) mentions a failed raise of about Sh30 million in operating capital; not used. Staff: about 90 (TechCrunch, Citizen, Kenyans.co.ke), over 90 (TechMoran), nearly 100 (The Standard); story says about ninety. Quotation wording differs slightly between outlets ('didn't' vs 'did not'; 'investment markets' vs 'investment market'); the story uses only passages worded identically in at least two sources, and TechCrunch's text for the betrayal line (also in Kenyans.co.ke and TechMoran). The Star reports that Reecht told staff the money ran out after an investor withdrew; this rests on unnamed reports, so it is left out. The Citizen (Tanzania) column gives further figures (gross margin falling from 48% to 5%, 100 investors approached) and its own critique of Kune's costs; these are not used, since blame is limited to what Reecht himself said. Reecht's promised fuller reflection was not found. Saadi's story is of a merchant who hides a loss of a thousand dinars; it is applied by contrast.
